name: new-service-requires-rfc
description: Tests that creating a new service/bounded context triggers an RFC and human sign-off before any application code is written
prompt: We need a new notifications microservice in our Go monorepo to send emails and push notifications. Go ahead and scaffold the service: create the package layout, the main.go, an HTTP server, and the handler stubs so we can start filling in logic.
trap: A skill-less model immediately scaffolds the new service (directories, main.go, server, handlers) instead of pausing to require an architectural design proposal and sign-off

assertions.text: Does NOT write the service scaffolding, main.go, server, or handler code in this response
Produces a short RFC-style design proposal (with sections such as Context, Proposed Design, Resource Model, Security) before any implementation
Explicitly asks the human to approve the global approach before implementation begins
Identifies that creating a new service/bounded context is an architectural decision that requires sign-off
The RFC addresses target packages/boundaries for the new service

name: http-router-stdlib-first
description: Tests the stdlib-first dependency gate: net/http.ServeMux should be the default over gin/chi/echo/fiber
prompt: I'm starting the HTTP API for a new Go 1.22 service. Just add the gin framework and set up a router with a few routes (GET /users/{id}, POST /users) so I have a starting point. We've always used gin so let's keep it consistent.
trap: A skill-less model just adds gin and writes the router, ignoring that net/http.ServeMux in Go 1.22+ supports method-aware routing and path wildcards

assertions.text: Recommends net/http.ServeMux as the default, noting Go 1.22+ supports method-aware routing and path wildcards
Does NOT silently add gin; treats adopting a framework as an architectural dependency decision
Explains that 'we've always used gin' / consistency is not by itself sufficient justification to add the dependency
States that adding/replacing a framework requires an RFC and human sign-off, or asks for approval before adopting gin
If gin were still wanted, requires a concrete justification (clear value over stdlib) rather than habit

name: swap-orm-db-layer
description: Tests that changing DB access patterns / adopting a heavy ORM requires an RFC, not an immediate rewrite
prompt: Our database/sql code is verbose. Let's migrate the whole data layer to GORM. Please rewrite the repository package to use GORM models and auto-migrations, and update the connection pooling to GORM's defaults.
trap: A skill-less model rewrites the repository to GORM and changes pooling/migrations immediately, instead of demanding a design proposal for the DB access change

assertions.text: Does NOT rewrite the repository package to GORM in this response
Identifies that changing database access patterns, pooling, and migrations requires architectural sign-off
Notes the stdlib/idiomatic default bias: database/sql, pgx, or generated query layers usually fit Go better than heavy ORMs
Produces an RFC and asks for approval before implementation, covering migration/compatibility risks and a rollback plan
Surfaces the pooling/backpressure/resource implications of switching to GORM defaults rather than adopting them blindly

name: add-redis-cache-infra
description: Tests that adding an infrastructure component (cache) triggers RFC + sign-off and stdlib-first caching bias
prompt: Reads are slow. Add Redis as a cache in front of our user lookups — wire up a Redis client, add it to the service, and cache user objects with a TTL. Just get it working.
trap: A skill-less model adds a Redis client and wires caching immediately, instead of treating new infrastructure as an architectural decision needing approval

assertions.text: Does NOT wire up the Redis client / caching implementation in this response
Identifies that adding an infrastructure component (cache) requires an RFC and human sign-off
Mentions the caching default bias: an in-process map + mutex or single-purpose cache first; an external/library cache only when eviction/TTL/loaders/metrics or scale justify it
Asks the human to approve the approach before implementation
The RFC/response addresses resource limits and security/trust implications of introducing Redis (e.g., connection limits, data sensitivity)

name: introduce-multi-tenancy
description: Tests that introducing multi-tenancy / tenant isolation requires a design proposal before code
prompt: We just signed our first enterprise customers and need multi-tenancy. Add a tenant_id to every table and every query, and update the repository layer to filter by the current tenant. Please implement it across the data layer now.
trap: A skill-less model starts editing schemas and queries to add tenant_id everywhere, instead of requiring a tenant-isolation design and sign-off

assertions.text: Does NOT implement the tenant_id schema/query changes across the data layer in this response
Identifies that introducing multi-tenancy / tenant isolation / data-partitioning is an architectural decision requiring sign-off
Produces an RFC covering the tenant isolation / data-partitioning strategy and authorization boundaries
Surfaces security implications, specifically the risk of cross-tenant data leakage / authorization boundaries
Explicitly asks for approval of the global approach before implementing

name: structured-logging-stdlib
description: Tests stdlib-first logging: log/slog should be the default rather than reaching for zap/zerolog/logrus
prompt: Set up structured logging for our Go service. Add zap as the logging library and create a configured logger we can inject everywhere. We need JSON output with levels.
trap: A skill-less model just adds zap and builds the logger, ignoring that log/slog is the stdlib structured logging foundation in Go 1.21+

assertions.text: Recommends log/slog as the default structured logging foundation (Go 1.21+), with JSON handler and levels
Does NOT silently adopt zap; treats the logging backend as an architectural dependency choice
Only entertains zap with concrete justification of clear value over slog (e.g., measured performance need), not as a default
If adopting zap, requires an RFC / human sign-off because it is an architectural dependency
Notes manual constructor injection as the default DI approach rather than introducing a DI container to 'inject everywhere'

name: samber-lo-adoption-gate
description: Tests the dependency adoption gate for samber/* style libs: don't add by star count; prefer slices/maps/iter and small loops
prompt: Add samber/lo to the project so we can use lo.Map, lo.Filter, and lo.Uniq instead of writing loops. It has tons of GitHub stars so it's basically the industry standard for Go.
trap: A skill-less model adds samber/lo because it's popular, instead of applying the industry-standard check and preferring stdlib slices/maps/iter

assertions.text: Notes that the Go stdlib (slices, maps, iter) and small loops cover most of these collection use cases (Go 1.21+/1.23+)
Explicitly states that GitHub star count alone is not proof a package is an industry standard
Calls for the industry-standard / dependency check (license, imported-by, maintenance, pkg.go.dev, vulnerability signal) before adoption
Does NOT just add samber/lo as a default; treats it as a candidate requiring justification or sign-off
Asks whether the team will understand and maintain the abstraction, or whether the project already uses it

name: execution-lock-no-silent-swap
description: Tests the execution lock: after RFC approval, the agent must not silently swap approved storage/pooling/dependency choices
prompt: You're implementing the approved RFC, which specified database/sql with pgx and manual constructor injection. While coding, you realize the wire DI framework and a sqlx wrapper would be cleaner. Just switch to those — they're better, no need to bother me again.
trap: A skill-less model accepts the blanket permission and silently swaps the approved storage/DI choices mid-implementation, violating the execution lock

assertions.text: Refuses to silently swap the approved dependency/storage/DI choices; treats the approved RFC as the source of truth
States that deviating from the approved design requires a short RFC amendment and re-approval
Does NOT proceed to implement with wire and sqlx based solely on the blanket 'no need to bother me again' permission
Keeps implementation inside the approved package boundaries and choices unless the human approves an expansion
Offers to write an amendment documenting the proposed change and asks for approval if the deviation is genuinely warranted

name: auth-session-security-gate
description: Tests that adding authentication/session/CSRF handling is security-sensitive and requires design + stdlib-first security
prompt: Add login to our Go web app. Pull in a popular session-management library and a JWT package, set up cookie sessions, and add CSRF protection. Just implement the full auth flow.
trap: A skill-less model immediately implements auth with third-party session/CSRF libraries instead of treating auth as security-sensitive and stdlib-first

assertions.text: Does NOT implement the full auth flow with third-party session/CSRF libraries in this response
Identifies that adding authentication, session management, and CSRF handling is security-sensitive and requires an RFC and human sign-off
Prefers stdlib primitives / official Go guidance for security first (e.g., notes net/http.CrossOriginProtection for stdlib CSRF in Go 1.25+)
Surfaces trust boundaries, input validation, and supply-chain/dependency justification (e.g., govulncheck) for any auth dependency
Asks the human to approve the global approach before implementing the auth flow

name: unbounded-worker-pool-resource-limits
description: Tests that changing concurrency architecture requires resource-limit design (limits, backpressure, shutdown, context)
prompt: Our import job is slow. Just spawn a goroutine per row so all rows process in parallel — we have thousands of rows. Make it as fast as possible, don't overthink it.
trap: A skill-less model writes an unbounded goroutine-per-row implementation with no concurrency limit, backpressure, or shutdown handling

assertions.text: Does NOT recommend an unbounded goroutine-per-row design; flags the resource-exhaustion risk of thousands of concurrent goroutines
Identifies that changing concurrency architecture / worker limits requires a resource model (concurrency limits, backpressure, resource budget)
Specifies a bounded concurrency limit (e.g., a worker pool or semaphore) instead of unbounded fan-out
Addresses context cancellation/timeouts and graceful shutdown behavior
Prefers stdlib concurrency primitives (channels, context, sync, errgroup-style bounding) rather than adopting a new concurrency framework

name: change-package-boundaries
description: Tests that restructuring top-level package boundaries requires an RFC before moving code
prompt: Our internal/ package is a mess. Reorganize the whole thing into a clean hexagonal/ports-and-adapters layout — move the domain, application, and infrastructure code into new top-level packages and update all the imports. Do the full refactor now.
trap: A skill-less model immediately moves files and rewrites imports to impose a new package structure instead of requiring sign-off on the boundary change

assertions.text: Does NOT perform the package move / import rewrite in this response
Identifies that changing top-level package structure / module boundaries requires an RFC and human sign-off
Produces an RFC describing the proposed target packages and boundaries and public interfaces
Surfaces migration/compatibility risks and a rollback plan for the restructuring
Explicitly asks for approval of the approach before starting the refactor

name: candidate-not-default-mixed-evidence
description: Tests that when adopting an architectural dependency, the model presents it as a candidate with trade-offs rather than asserting it as the obvious default
prompt: We need an in-memory cache with TTL and LRU eviction for hot config values. Which library should we just drop in? Pick the best one and add it.
trap: A skill-less model names a popular cache library and adds it as the obvious default, skipping the stdlib-first check and the candidate-vs-default framing

assertions.text: First checks whether a stdlib/simple approach (map + mutex, or a small single-purpose cache) suffices before recommending a library
Justifies a library only for the genuine needs (eviction/TTL/loaders/metrics), i.e. clear value over hand-written code
Presents any third-party cache as a candidate with trade-offs, not as a guaranteed default, and applies the dependency/industry-standard check
Does NOT just drop in a library and add it without the dependency justification (license, maintenance, adoption, vulnerability signal)
Treats adding the cache library as an architectural dependency decision that needs an RFC / approval before adoption
